tip: English makes 'students' the subject of 'were given'. Hindi doesn't: छात्रों को (chhatron ko = to the students) stays, and दी गई (di gai) agrees with वर्दी (vardi = uniform).
बनी है (bani hai) is not a passive – it's बनना (banna = to get made). Hindi often says 'the library became' where English needs 'was built', no जाना (jana) involved.
No stated doer: मानते हैं (maante hain = [people] consider) leaves out who considers. Where English says 'is considered', Hindi often just drops the 'they'.
A sentence is announced aloud in Hindi: सज़ा सुनाई गई (saza sunai gai) is literally 'the punishment was made heard' – सुनाना (sunana) means to make someone hear.
बनवाया (banvaya) is not plain 'built' – the -वा- (-va-) means the Mughals had it built by others. बनाया (banaya) = built it yourself; बनवाया = got it built.
जाने से मना है (jane se mana hai) is literally 'there is refusal from going' – the banned action takes से (se = from). That's the standard 'not allowed' pattern on signs.
Completed actions usually mark the doer with ने: मैंने (maine = I). The verb then agrees with the object – निकाले (nikaale) is plural for पैसे (paise = money), not for 'I'.
Hugging is neck-based: गले लगाया (gale lagaya) is literally 'attached to the neck'. गला (gala) means the neck-throat area – that's where the hug happens.
You give an exam in Hindi to take it: परीक्षा दी (pariksha di = gave the exam). The examiner is the one who takes it – परीक्षा ली (pariksha li). Reversed from English.
Adding जी (ji) shows respect or warmth: दादाजी (dadaji = respected grandfather). Elders often get it built in – पिताजी (pitaji), माताजी (mataji).
No ने (ne) here – बचाती है (bachati hai = saves) is a habit, and ने only marks completed past actions. Present-tense doers stay plain: गीता (Geeta), not गीता ने.
Even in the past, ने (ne) skips motion verbs: चली गई (chali gayi = went off) takes no ने. Only verbs that act on an object use it.
English words become Hindi verbs through किया (kiya = did): बुक किया (book kiya) = booked. Same pattern for फ़ोन किया (phone kiya) and ऑर्डर किया (order kiya).
Bills get filled, not paid: बिल भर दिया (bill bhar diya = filled the bill). भरना (bharna = to fill) covers paying bills, fees and fines.
Adding दिया (diya = gave) to a verb means done for someone else: गरम कर दिया (garam kar diya) – heated it for me. With लिया (liya = took) it would be for herself.
Hindi skips 'get' – things turn up instead: मिलेगा (milega = will be found). You ask where the ticket will be found, not where you can get it.
रुक जाएगी (ruk jaayegi) adds जाना (jaana = to go) to 'stop' – the go-verb marks a complete change: the rain won't just pause, it will stop for good.
Future verbs carry gender: दुकान (dukaan = shop) is feminine, so it खुलेगी (khulegi), ending in -egi. A masculine subject would take खुलेगा (khulega).
चलोगे (chaloge) is an invite: चलना (chalna) means going along together, so this asks 'coming to the market with me?' Going on your own is जाना (jaana).
Polite offers use 'take', not 'have': चाय लेंगे? (chaay lenge? = will you take tea?). Future + लेना (lena) is the standard courteous way to offer.
डेढ़ (dedh) is one word meaning exactly 'one and a half' – Hindi gives 1.5 and 2.5 their own words (ढाई / dhaai = 2.5) rather than phrases.
One doctor, plural verb: देखेंगे (dekhenge) is the respectful plural. Singular देखेगा (dekhega) here would sound rude – respect makes one person grammatically plural.
In Hindi directions, landmarks come to you: अस्पताल आएगा (aspataal aayega = the hospital will come). You don't find it – after the turn, it shows up.
'The more... the more' needs a matched pair: जितनी मेहनत करोगे (jitni mehnat karoge), उतना फल मिलेगा (utna phal milega) – jitni sets it up, utna answers it.
The if-half of a future condition often uses a past form: अगर मौसम अच्छा रहा (agar mausam achchha raha = if the weather stayed good). Only चलेंगे (chalenge) is future.
भेज दूँगा (bhej doonga) adds देना (dena = to give) to 'send' – the give-helper marks doing it for someone else, a favor tone plain भेजूँगा (bhejoonga) lacks.
You ask FROM someone in Hindi – शिक्षक से सवाल पूछा (shikshak se sawaal poochha): से (se = from) marks the person asked, not को (ko).
In न सिर्फ़...बल्कि (na sirf...balki = not only...but rather), the 'also' splits off – भी (bhi) lands after the new item: पहला नंबर भी (pahla number bhi).
To lead with the reason, use चूँकि (choonki = since), answered by इसलिए (isliye = so): चूँकि बारिश हो रही थी, इसलिए... क्योंकि (kyonki = because) usually follows the main clause instead.
After ताकि (taaki = so that), the verb takes its wish form – उठ सकूँ (uth sakoon), not the plain future उठूँगा (uthoonga).
